terms.plain: The part of a return that cannot be explained by simply carrying market risk. It is the bit you are actually paying a manager for, and it is much rarer than marketing material suggests.
terms.formal: The component of return in excess of that predicted by an asset pricing model given the portfolio's systematic risk exposures.

terms.plain: How much a portfolio moves when the market moves. A beta of 0.7 means it tends to move about 70% as much as the market, up or down.
terms.formal: A measure of an asset's sensitivity to movements in a reference market, equal to the covariance of asset and market returns divided by the variance of market returns.

terms.plain: Public markets fall, private marks do not move, so the private allocation rises as a share of a smaller portfolio. A measurement artefact that forces real selling.
terms.formal: The mechanical increase in an illiquid asset allocation caused by a decline in the value of liquid holdings while illiquid valuations remain stale.

terms.plain: How far an investment has fallen from its highest previous value. A 20% drawdown means you are 20% below the best it has ever been.
terms.formal: The peak-to-trough decline in cumulative value over a specified period, expressed as a percentage of the prior peak.

terms.plain: The average loss on the days that breach your value-at-risk threshold. Strictly more informative than VaR, and less widely quoted because it is less flattering.
terms.formal: The conditional expectation of loss given that loss exceeds the value-at-risk threshold at a specified confidence level.

terms.plain: A portfolio's tilt toward a broad characteristic — small companies, cheap companies, fast-growing companies, recent winners. Often unintentional, and dangerous precisely because it is invisible until it reverses.
terms.formal: The sensitivity of a portfolio's returns to a systematic risk factor, measured as the coefficient on that factor in a multi-factor return model.

terms.plain: Alpha divided by its volatility — how much skill per unit of noise. It sets how many years of data are needed before a track record means anything: (1.96 / IR)² years.
terms.formal: Active return divided by tracking error, measuring risk-adjusted outperformance relative to a benchmark.

terms.plain: Breaking a return apart to see where it actually came from — which positions, which side of the book, how much was just the market rising.
terms.formal: The decomposition of portfolio return into contributions from identifiable sources such as allocation, selection, systematic factor exposures and residual effects.

terms.plain: Return above the risk-free rate, divided by volatility. It asks how much return you got for each unit of bounce you had to endure.
terms.formal: Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of excess returns. Penalises volatility symmetrically, so it treats upside and downside variation alike.

terms.plain: A loss level you would not expect to exceed, at some stated confidence. Its weakness is that it says nothing at all about how bad things get beyond that point.
terms.formal: The loss threshold not expected to be exceeded over a given horizon at a stated confidence level. Silent about the severity of losses in the excluded tail, and understated when returns have fat tails.

terms.plain: How much a return series bounces around. It is just the standard deviation of returns, usually quoted per year.
terms.formal: The annualised standard deviation of returns. Monthly figures scale by the square root of twelve, since variances rather than standard deviations are additive over time.
